previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with T1-T2 paraplegia, chronic obstructive lung disease, and a history of recurrent pneumonia and UTIs, was admitted with shortness of breath, fever, and hypoxia. She was found to have a urinary tract infection caused by multidrug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, sensitive only to meropenem, and aspiration pneumonia with MRSA involvement. She was initially managed in the MICU with vancomycin and meropenem, along with supportive care for respiratory failure. Due to difficult IV access, a tunneled central line was placed after failed PICC attempts. A video swallow study confirmed aspiration with thin and nectar-thick liquids, leading to dietary modifications. Her condition improved with treatment, oxygen requirements returned to baseline, and she was discharged home with a plan to complete a 10-day course of IV antibiotics via home health. Follow-up was arranged with pulmonology and gastroenterology.

admission for pna.  Pt reports that she believes that she 
aspirated some of her food on the morning of admission.  She 
then spiked a fever in the ED and had worsening SOB.  The time 
course for aspiration event would favor chemical pneumonitis 
because development of aspiration pna is days, not hours.  
However, pt does appear to have PNA on CXR and was recently 
hospitalized for PNA so she was initiated on broad spectrum 
antibiotics for HCAP.  In the ICU she was started on 
vanc/cefepime/tobramycin/flagyl.  Her O2 requirement improved to 
her baseline of 2L and she was transferred to the floor.  On the 
floor, pt remained afebrile and hemodynamically stable.  She

tobramycin were d/ced on the floor, and sputum ultimately grew

additional 6 days of vancomycin for ten day course.
